lead: A wireless station cannot hear collisions while it transmits, and two stations that cannot hear each other may still collide at the access point. IEEE 802.11 therefore uses carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA): sense the radio channel, wait a fixed gap, back off a random number of slots, then send and demand an acknowledgement. Optional RTS/CTS frames reserve the channel and silence hidden stations. This is the MAC of Wi-Fi in homes, offices and campuses.
prereq: You need: 3.7 for CSMA/CA basics and 3.8 for the wired LAN it replaces.

blocks.text: An 802.11 network is built from a basic service set (BSS): one access point (AP) plus the stations that associate with it. The AP is the bridge between the radio cell and the wired network. A station joins by association after hearing the AP's beacon frames. The network name carried in management frames is the SSID, a text string such as HomeWiFi. In infrastructure mode all traffic goes through the AP, even station-to-station traffic in the same cell.
An independent BSS (IBSS) has no AP; stations talk directly. This is ad-hoc mode, used for a quick link between two laptops. A single BSS covers one radio range, typically tens of metres indoors.

An extended service set (ESS) joins several BSSs through a distribution system (DS), usually a wired Ethernet backbone. All APs in one ESS share the SSID, so a laptop can move from one cell to another; roaming is the station re-associating with a stronger AP, handled below the IP layer.

802.11 defines two coordination functions. Distributed coordination function (DCF) is mandatory and is plain CSMA/CA. Point coordination function (PCF) is an optional polled mode; most products do not use it.

items: Sense the medium. If it is idle for DIFS (DCF interframe space), go to step 3.
If it is busy, wait until it becomes idle, then wait DIFS again.
Choose a random backoff integer from 0 to CW, where CW is the contention window, counted in slots. Freeze the counter while the medium is busy; resume when the medium is idle for DIFS.
When the counter reaches 0, transmit one frame.
The receiver waits SIFS (short interframe space) and returns an ACK.

blocks.text: Interframe spaces are priorities: SIFS < PIFS < DIFS. Typical 802.11b values are SIFS = 10 μs, one slot = 20 μs, DIFS = 50 μs. Because SIFS is shorter than DIFS, the receiver's ACK starts before any other station is allowed to contend.
An ACK is required because a radio cannot listen while transmitting; CSMA/CD's collision detection is impossible. A missing ACK triggers retransmission.

Hidden terminal: A and C both hear the AP but not each other. Both sense idle, both send, and collide at the AP. Virtual carrier sensing fixes this. A frame carries a duration field. Any station that hears it sets its network allocation vector (NAV) to that duration and stays quiet, even if its own radio senses idle.

RTS/CTS four-way handshake: the sender sends Request to Send (RTS), the AP replies Clear to Send (CTS), then DATA, then ACK. Both RTS and CTS carry a duration covering the rest of the exchange. A station that hears the CTS knows the channel is reserved. RTS/CTS costs overhead, so it is used only for large frames or when hidden nodes are suspected. It removes the hidden-terminal collision, not every collision.

An 802.11 data frame has frame control (type, subtype, flags), duration, address 1, address 2, address 3, sequence control, frame body (payload) and FCS. In the common infrastructure case the three addresses are: address 1 = immediate receiver (the AP for an uplink frame), address 2 = transmitter (the station), address 3 = the eventual destination or the source. A fourth address appears only in a wireless distribution system.

Physical layers are named only here. The original 802.11 used DSSS at 1–2 Mbps in 2.4 GHz. 802.11b uses DSSS/CCK at up to 11 Mbps in 2.4 GHz; 802.11a uses OFDM at up to 54 Mbps in 5 GHz; 802.11g uses OFDM at up to 54 Mbps in 2.4 GHz.

figure.caption: The station waits 150 μs (DIFS 50 μs + 5 backoff slots × 20 μs) before sending a 727.27 μs frame; the ACK starts one SIFS (10 μs) later, at 887.27 μs. Notice the backoff and the total time.

spec.aria: Flowchart of the worked example: wait DIFS 50 μs, back off 5 slots (100 μs), transmit 727.27 μs, wait SIFS 10 μs, ACK starts at 887.27 μs.

examples.question: A station has a 1000-byte frame ready and the medium is idle. SIFS = 10 μs, DIFS = 50 μs, one backoff slot = 20 μs, and the station draws a backoff of 5 slots. The PHY rate is 11 Mbps. Find the wait before transmission, the frame transmission time, and the time from the medium going idle until the ACK starts. Ignore ACK transmission time and preamble.
steps: Wait = DIFS + 5 slots × 20 μs = 50 μs + 100 μs = 150 μs.
ACK starts one SIFS after the frame ends: total = 150 μs + 727.27 μs + 10 μs = 887.27 μs.
examples.answer: The station waits 150 μs, the frame takes 727.27 μs, and the ACK starts 887.27 μs after the medium went idle.
examples.check:
b = 1000
bits = b * 8
rate = 11_000_000
sifs = 10
difs = 50
slot = 20
slots = 5
wait_us = difs + slots * slot
frame_us = bits / rate * 1e6
total_us = wait_us + frame_us + sifs
print(wait_us)
print(round(frame_us, 2))
print(round(total_us, 2))

traps: Radio cannot hear collisions while sending, so 802.11 needs ACKs; Ethernet CSMA/CD does not.
A busy medium freezes the backoff counter; it does not reset it.
SIFS is shorter than DIFS so the ACK wins; do not swap the two.
RTS/CTS removes the hidden-terminal collision, not every collision.
Address 1 is the immediate receiver, not necessarily the final destination.

quiz.q: Name the two coordination functions of 802.11 and say which is mandatory.
quiz.a: DCF (distributed coordination function) is mandatory; PCF (point coordination function) is optional.

quiz.q: What is an SSID, and what is an AP?
quiz.a: SSID is the network name in management frames. An AP is the access point that bridges one radio cell to the wired network.

A radio cannot listen while transmitting, so a station cannot detect a collision at its own antenna. Hidden terminals make collisions happen at the receiver, not at the sender. 802.11 therefore avoids collisions and uses ACKs.

quiz.q: Why is SIFS shorter than DIFS?
quiz.a: SIFS gives the receiver's ACK priority over new contenders, which must wait DIFS. The ACK therefore starts before any other station can begin its backoff.

quiz.q: SIFS = 10 μs, DIFS = 50 μs, one slot = 20 μs. A station draws a backoff of 3 slots. How long does it wait after the medium is found idle?
A 1000-byte frame is sent at 54 Mbps. Find the frame transmission time.
A and C are hidden from each other but both hear the AP. Explain how RTS/CTS prevents a collision at the AP.
quiz.a: A sends RTS; the AP hears it and replies CTS. C hears the CTS, reads its duration field, sets its NAV and stays silent. A then sends DATA without C transmitting, so no collision occurs at the AP.

quiz.q: Why does freezing the backoff counter while the medium is busy help fairness?
quiz.a: A station that has already waited keeps its remaining count instead of losing it. It does not restart from a new random value each time another station transmits, so it cannot be starved and the waiting time is shared.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern Wi-Fi uses 802.11ac and 802.11ax, which add wider channels, MU-MIMO and OFDMA. Security has moved from WEP to WPA2 and WPA3. Search for 802.11ax OFDMA and WPA3 handshake to see how the ideas here scale.
